blocks.content: This skills lab is about finding a pace you can control and repeat. Do not deliberately lock a wheel, drift into a corner, or ride to the point where the front tire starts to slide. Those are poor targets for an unsupervised gravel drill.

### Start below the edge

Good bike handling is easier to build when you have time to notice what happened. Pick a flat, open, traffic-free place with a clear runout. Check the surface, tires, and brakes. Begin at walking pace. A controlled turn or stop tells you more than a near-crash at speed because you can repeat it and change one thing.

The useful limit for today is the point where you can no longer make the movement calmly. If you tense up, lose the line, or need an abrupt correction, make the task easier. The goal is to finish with a movement you can repeat, not a skid you survived.

blocks.label: Room to choose
blocks.content: In a slow, wide turn, look through the exit and notice whether you could widen the line or stop if something changed. Your hands should stay secure without pulling hard on the bars. You should be able to explain where you would go if the surface surprised you. If you cannot, widen the turn or slow down.

blocks.title: The Control Ladder
blocks.description: Build difficulty only when the previous step stays calm and repeatable.

steps.detail: Flat ground, no traffic, a visible surface, and plenty of runout.
Make a wide turn or a smooth stop at walking pace.
Use the same line and pace until the movement feels predictable.
Try a slightly different line or surface at the same easy pace. Do not add speed to force an outcome.
If a tire pushes, a wheel locks, or you need a rescue input, return to the easier version or end the session.

blocks.title: Wide Turn and Smooth Stop
blocks.description: Alternate a broad figure-eight with a straight-line stop in an empty area. Keep every repetition slow enough to do again without a skid.

variants.label: Two simple movements
steps: Place two markers far apart so you can make broad turns without leaning sharply.
Ride around each marker at a comfortable pace, looking toward the next open space.
On a separate straight section, squeeze both brakes gradually to a stop.
Write down what felt smooth and what made you tense. Repeat the easy version before changing the route.

variants.label: One visible surface change
steps: Choose a second, clearly visible surface in the same open area. Leave out wet, hidden, or highly loose patches.
Ride the same broad line at the same comfortable pace. Note how the steering and braking feel differ.
If the bike slides, squirms, or needs an abrupt correction, return to the easier surface and stop the comparison.

proof_gate.description: You can repeat a broad turn and gradual stop while leaving room to change your line.
proof_gate.target: Consistent, calm movements with no deliberate skid or speed target

blocks.title: When the practice stops feeling controlled

scenarios.label: Wheel lock or tire push
scenarios.situation: A wheel stops rolling or the bike begins to drift off the chosen line.
steps: Avoid another abrupt input. Look toward open space and ease the brake or steering demand that unsettled the bike.
Once stopped safely, check the bike and surface.
End the drill or restart at a slower pace with a wider line. Do not use the slide as a progress marker.

blocks.question: During a low-speed practice turn, the front tire begins to push. What should you do with the drill?

options.text: Stop safely, check the surface, and return to a wider or slower turn
Repeat faster so you can learn the true lean-angle limit
Lock the rear wheel to steer through the turn
Keep tightening the markers until the slide is repeatable

blocks.explanation: The slide tells you the current exercise has become less controlled. Reset to an easier line or pace. Deliberate skids and lean limits are not goals for this unsupervised drill.

blocks.content: Do one short session of wide turns and smooth stops in an empty area. Record the line and pace that felt repeatable. If you had to rescue a turn, make the next attempt easier.
